content: D.D. Palmer, born on March 7, 1845, in Pickering, Ontario, Canada, near Toronto, was the founder of chiropractic. His parents were Katherine McVay and Thomas Palmer. At the age of twenty, he moved to the United States with his family. Over the years, Palmer worked in various professions, including as a beekeeper, school teacher, and grocery store owner. He developed a keen interest in the health philosophies of his time, such as magnetic healing and Spiritualism. In the mid-1880s, Palmer began practicing magnetic healing in Burlington, Iowa, and later in Davenport, Iowa. He was an avid reader of medical journals and closely followed global developments in anatomy and physiology. While working as a magnetic healer in Davenport, he encountered a deaf janitor who had a palpable lump in his back. Palmer hypothesized that the lump and the man’s deafness were connected. After reportedly restoring the man’s hearing, this event marked the beginning of chiropractic history. Palmer’s theories centered on the idea that altered nerve flow was the root cause of all diseases and that misaligned spinal vertebrae disrupted this nerve flow. He proposed that restoring proper alignment to the vertebrae would restore health. In 1897, Palmer founded a school based on his work, which later became the Palmer School of Chiropractic. By 1902, the school had graduated 15 chiropractors. In 1906, Palmer was prosecuted under Iowa’s new medical arts law for practicing medicine without a license. He chose to serve 17 days in jail rather than pay the fine but eventually decided to pay it. Shortly after, he sold the chiropractic school to his son, B.J. Palmer. Following this, D.D. Palmer moved to the West Coast, where he helped establish chiropractic schools in Oklahoma, California, and Oregon. However, his relationship with his son B.J. was strained and often contentious, particularly after the sale of the school. The circumstances surrounding Palmer’s death in 1913 remain controversial. During a Founder’s Day parade in Davenport, Iowa, in August 1913, Palmer was reportedly struck from behind by a car driven by his son, B.J. Some denied this claim. Palmer died on October 20, 1913, in Los Angeles, California. The official cause of death was typhoid fever, though some speculated it was related to injuries from the alleged incident. Courts exonerated B.J. of any responsibility for his father’s death. D.D. Palmer held subjective and personal religious beliefs. As an active spiritualist, he claimed to have received chiropractic from the other world through inspiration from a deceased medical physician named Dr. Jim Atkinson. According to B.J. Palmer, D.D. first received messages from Dr. Atkinson regarding the principles of chiropractic during séances, though D.D. stated he received them through inspiration. In his posthumously published book, The Chiropractor (1914), Palmer described chiropractic as partially religious in nature. He emphasized the moral and religious duty of chiropractors and discussed religious liberty. However, he later distanced himself from formally renaming chiropractic as a religion, instead distinguishing between formal, objective religion and personal, subjective ethical beliefs. Palmer faced significant opposition during his lifetime and was often accused of being a crank and a quack. His book, The Chiropractor’s Adjuster (also known as The Text-Book of the Science, Art, and Philosophy of Chiropractic), was published in 1910 by the Portland Printing House Company in Oregon and reprinted in 1966 by his grandson, David D. Palmer. In this book, Palmer famously stated, There is a vast difference between treating effects and adjusting the causes.
